name: Erbium YAG resurfacing

lead: Er:YAG resurfacing removes thin layers of skin to smooth acne scars, deep wrinkles and pigment such as melasma. It is described as a gentler-heat alternative to CO2.

The 2940 nm beam is strongly absorbed by water and ablates shallow layers with limited heat spreading into surrounding tissue. Wikipedia says this gives a lower risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than CO2. Much of the early Er:YAG research concerns dental tissue; skin trials in the sources are small registrations covering skin aging, acne scars with PRP and cutaneous neurofibromas.

paras: It is done in a clinic, in one session or a short series depending on the depth wanted. Skin typically looks pink and peels while it heals, with a recovery that depends on settings. It is sometimes combined with other treatments for acne scars.

Reported risks of laser resurfacing include scarring, pigment change, acne and herpes outbreaks. Redness, swelling and peeling are expected during healing. People prone to cold sores, scarring or pigment changes should discuss this with the provider.

chain: Skin heals with less heat damage
Smoother texture, fewer scars and wrinkles
angle.text: Er:YAG removes thin layers of skin with a water-absorbing laser, so skin heals with less heat damage and ends up smoother, with fewer scars and wrinkles. It is used for acne scars, deep wrinkles and melasma, and is described as shallower than CO2.

lead: Erbium:YAG (Er:YAG) resurfacing uses a 2940 nm laser, strongly absorbed by water, to remove thin layers of skin for acne scars, deep wrinkles and melasma [1][2]. Wikipedia says Er:YAG lasers carry a lower risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than CO2 lasers because they produce less heat [2].

Much of the early Er:YAG research concerns dental hard tissue and periodontal use rather than skin, such as 1989 ablation-rate studies [3][4]. Skin-specific trials in the sources are small registrations covering skin aging, acne scars with PRP, and cutaneous neurofibromas [5][6][7].

paras: Er:YAG lasers emit infrared light at about 2940 nm, strongly absorbed by water, giving shallow tissue effects [1]. They are used in resurfacing for acne scarring, deep rhytides and melasma [1]. Fractional variants, discussed in a 2006 review of fractional photothermolysis applications, extend the approach [8].

Wikipedia states that CO2 produces higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers [2]. Reported complications of laser resurfacing in general include scarring, hyperpigmentation, acne and herpes outbreaks [2].

A 151-person study registered in 2007 evaluated safety and efficacy of erbium treatment for skin aging [5]. A 32-person study combined lasers and PRP for post-acne scars [6], and a phase 2/3 study examined Er:YAG vaporization of cutaneous neurofibromas [7]. A sham-controlled trial compared Er:YAG with the CO2RE intimate laser for vaginal atrophy [9]. Results are not summarised in the registrations cited here.

timeline.event: Early laboratory studies of Er:YAG ablation of dental hard tissue published [3][4].
